card: A president at sea when the crisis breaks. Will you hold on to Russia, or let go?
intro: You are Raymond Poincaré, President of the French Third Republic. Born in 1860 at Bar-le-Duc in Lorraine, you saw your hometown occupied by Prussian troops when you were ten, and watched France lose Alsace-Lorraine in 1871. After careers as a lawyer, finance minister and prime minister, you were elected president in January 1913 (taking office in February). Under the constitution every act of the president needs a minister’s countersignature, but Viviani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister, has almost no diplomatic experience, so in practice it is you who sets the course of French foreign policy. Your ambassador in St Petersburg is your old school friend Maurice Paléologue, and in London the seasoned Paul Cambon; in Paris you have Joseph Joffre, chief of the general staff, and Adolphe Messimy, the war minister. France is allied with Russia; with Britain it has only the Entente Cordiale, which carries no obligation to fight side by side.

FR-00.place: Presidential stand, Longchamp racecourse, Bois de Boulogne, Paris
FR-00.title: The Telegram at Longchamp

telegram.text: Austrian heir Archduke Franz Ferdinand and wife Duchess of Hohenberg shot during visit to Sarajevo / two attacks / both dead

FR-00.scene: On the afternoon of Sunday, 28 June 1914, you have come with your wife Henriette, as custom requires, to watch the Grand Prix at Longchamp. Under a clear sky, cheerful crowds line the avenues of the Bois de Boulogne, and the presidential stand holds the presidents of the Senate and the Chamber and the foreign diplomatic corps. In the middle of the racing a Havas telegram is brought to you. There is no official confirmation yet, but the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, Count Szécsen, is sitting close by. Every diplomat in the stand is watching to see how the president handles the news.

voices.text: This crime will give Austria a pretext for war. There are many in Vienna who would like to settle accounts with Serbia.
The Archduke’s children were already barred from the succession by his morganatic marriage. What worries us more is what becomes of the Habsburg monarchy after the old emperor.

choices.text: Leave the races for the Élysée at once, summon Viviani and senior Foreign Ministry staff, and have them track Vienna’s response
choices.why: France must read the situation before Vienna and Berlin do
choices.after: Your hasty departure told the diplomats in the stand that France regarded the affair as a grave crisis. The next day the newspapers vied with one another to describe your grim face, and the Vienna papers asked mockingly what France had to worry about.

choices.text: Hand the telegram to Ambassador Szécsen first, stay to the end of the racing to show no alarm, then send condolences to Vienna
choices.why: Keeping to protocol and showing calm serves France best
choices.after: Szécsen, white-faced, left to await official word at his embassy, and since the other ambassadors stayed, you had to remain beside them until the racing ended. Back at the Élysée you at once sent a telegram of condolence to Franz Joseph, and on Monday you received the emperor’s courteous reply. At the cabinet meeting of 30 June Austria came up only briefly; the question of the religious congregations took far longer.

choices.text: To deny Vienna a pretext, advise Pašić’s government through the French minister in Belgrade to cooperate promptly with the inquiry
choices.why: If Serbia cooperates first, Vienna loses its pretext
choices.after: The Pašić government received the French advice politely, but with elections due in August it was reluctant to dig into an affair that might implicate officers of its own army. St Petersburg was uneasy that Paris was pressing Serbia so early.

note.text: Franz Joseph never forgave his nephew’s morganatic marriage, and Vienna invited no foreign sovereigns or diplomatic delegations to the funeral. Wilhelm II had meant to attend, but according to Dumaine, the French ambassador in Vienna, he stayed at Potsdam, citing a slight illness.

FR-00a.time: Afternoon, after a luncheon for the generals
FR-00a.title: Go or Stay
FR-00a.clock: About 32 hours until the presidential train leaves for Dunkirk (11:30 p.m., 15 July)
FR-00a.event: On 13 July, in the Senate, Charles Humbert, rapporteur of the army committee, laid bare one gap after another in the country’s armaments: a special defense bill of 420 million francs, tabled in February 1913, had still not been passed. War Minister Messimy answered him, but the Senate’s alarm did not subside, and the debate has run on into the afternoon of 14 July, Bastille Day. On 5 July Ambassador Szécsen had called at the Élysée to convey the emperor’s thanks for your condolences, adding that Serbia had long been inciting the Slavs against the monarchy.
FR-00a.scene: This morning there was a military review at Longchamp, and on the way there and back the crowds in the Bois de Boulogne cheered with unusual warmth. After lunch Abel Ferry, the Foreign Ministry’s under-secretary of state, brings a message from Viviani: Clemenceau is about to join Humbert in calling for a Senate commission of inquiry, and Viviani wants your view. Tomorrow night you and Viviani set out on a long tour of Russia and the three Scandinavian kingdoms. The tour has been six months in the planning and parliament has voted the funds, but no one knows what Vienna is preparing. And on 20 July, while you are at sea, the trial of Madame Caillaux opens at the Paris assize court.

voices.who: You (looking back on this day in your memoirs)
voices.text: If I now changed my intention, I would risk making people believe that danger was imminent, and alarming Europe.
For years the government has covered up the army’s deficiencies. Unless the Senate investigates for itself, nothing will be put right.
This tour has been more than five months in the making. To put it off now would invite the worst construction, and France would seem to be stirring up a crisis that no one can yet see.

choices.text: As Jaurès urged in the Chamber, postpone the Russian tour and stay in Paris until Vienna’s intentions are known
choices.why: No head of state leaves his capital while Vienna’s intentions are hidden
choices.after: The Élysée announced that the tour would be put off for some weeks because of parliamentary business. The Russian court was deeply disappointed, and newspapers across Europe began to ask what France knew that kept its president in Paris.

choices.text: Block Clemenceau’s inquiry as an abdication of government, and leave as planned on the Russian tour six months in the making
choices.why: A sudden change of schedule would only feed a crisis
choices.after: You told Abel Ferry that setting up an inquiry would mean the government abdicating its own responsibility, and at about 10:30 p.m. you heard that Clemenceau had withdrawn his motion and the army committee would write a detailed report instead. On the night of 15 July your wife Henriette decided to await your return at Sampigny in the Meuse, and at 11:30 p.m. you boarded the train at the Gare du Nord with Viviani and Navy Minister Gauthier. Before dawn on 16 July the battleship France weighed anchor at Dunkirk.

note.text: Vienna decided to hand over its ultimatum only after Poincaré had left St Petersburg. When Ambassador Tschirschky reported this decision to Berlin on 14 July, Wilhelm II wrote in the margin of the report: 'What a pity!'

pressure.title: Unfinished Business
pressure.text: On the morning of 16 March, the day Calmette was killed, Caillaux took you aside just before the cabinet meeting and shouted that he would kill Calmette if the paper printed his and his wife’s private letters; you have testified to this conversation under oath. In January of that year, at Caillaux’s request, you had also stopped Calmette from publishing the so-called 'green documents.' These were decrypts of three German diplomatic telegrams exposing secret negotiations by Caillaux’s side during the Agadir crisis of 1911, typed on pale green paper, hence the name. On 11 July Caillaux pressed you, saying he had proof that you had been behind the press campaign against him and would make it public unless you worked for his wife’s acquittal. If you postpone the tour, people will say the president stayed in Paris with an eye on the trial.

FR-01P.title: The President Who Stayed
FR-01P.scene: It is the second day of Madame Caillaux’s trial, and the Paris papers are full of courtroom reports. Your sworn account of what Caillaux told you privately before the cabinet meeting on the morning of 16 March has gone into the record of the case word for word. Vienna, meanwhile, is silent, and Ambassador Szécsen is as courteous as ever. Dumaine, the ambassador in Vienna, reports that the old emperor will hold back the hard-liners, but with you still in Paris, nothing tells you what Vienna is waiting for.

voices.text: Your remaining here is enough to make Vienna and Berlin reconsider. If we act in haste now, it will be said that France made the crisis.
His Majesty the Tsar is hurt that the tour was postponed. He looks for a clear word on how France regards the alliance.

choices.text: Summon Ambassador Szécsen and warn him in advance that harsh demands on Serbia would alarm Russia and her friends
choices.why: A warning works only if it comes before Vienna decides
choices.after: Szécsen only repeated that the judicial inquiry was under way, and withdrew. That night a report went to Vienna that the French president was taking a close interest in the Serbian question.

choices.text: Instruct Paul Cambon to propose to Grey a joint framework for great-power mediation before Vienna’s demands appear
choices.why: Only with Britain at France’s side can this crisis be managed
choices.after: Grey welcomed the idea but put off formal talks, saying nothing had happened yet. Still, the foreign ministries in London and Paris agreed to inform each other at once if a crisis broke.

choices.text: As Izvolsky asks, have him tell the Tsar that with the president staying in Paris, Russia can rely on France
choices.why: The hurt over the delayed tour must be made good with firm words
choices.after: Izvolsky wired Sazonov at once. The war party in St Petersburg forgot its disappointment over the postponed tour and became convinced of French support.

note.text: Vienna did in fact hold back delivery of the ultimatum until Poincaré was leaving Russia. On 18 July the Bavarian chargé d’affaires in Berlin also reported home that Vienna was waiting for Poincaré and Viviani to depart, so that the two allies could not agree on a joint response.

FR-02P.title: 48 Hours
FR-02P.clock: About 33 hours until Serbia’s deadline (6 p.m., 25 July)
FR-02P.event: Even with the president in Paris, Vienna did not wait. At 6 p.m. on 23 July the Austro-Hungarian minister, Giesl, handed Belgrade an ultimatum with a 48-hour deadline.
FR-02P.scene: In a conference room at the Quai d’Orsay, you, Viviani and Berthelot of the political department read the text of the ultimatum together. Of its ten demands, point 5 requires Serbia to accept the collaboration of Austrian officials in suppressing the anti-Austrian movement, and point 6 requires Austrian officials to take part in a judicial inquiry on Serbian soil. In London Grey has not yet moved, and reports from St Petersburg say Sazonov has spoken of a European war. Unlike in the July crisis as it actually unfolded, everyone who makes French foreign policy is in Paris this morning.

voices.text: Serbia should accept almost every demand and refer the rest to international arbitration. Above all, we must gain time.
Vienna has already made up its mind. If diplomacy drags on while our mobilization preparations fall behind, we will pay for it on the frontier.

choices.text: Follow Berthelot’s plan: with Britain, demand a longer deadline, and urge Serbia to accept as much as it possibly can
choices.why: The more Serbia yields, the weaker Vienna’s case becomes
choices.after: The advice from Paris reached Belgrade at almost the same moment as London’s. On 25 July Serbia accepted most of the demands and rejected point 6, and Giesl left Belgrade that evening.

choices.text: Accept Messimy’s view that Vienna has decided: tell Russia France will stand with her to the end, and protest sharply to Vienna
choices.why: Vienna has decided, and only force can stop it now
choices.after: Izvolsky passed your words to St Petersburg exactly as spoken, and the Russian council of ministers took up military preparations, sure of French support. Vienna heard the French protest as Russia’s own voice.

choices.text: Have Paris be first to propose four-power mediation, and require Russia to consult Paris before taking any military step
choices.why: France must lead the mediation or be dragged along by it
choices.after: Grey backed the French proposal at once, but Berlin put off its answer, calling the dispute a matter for Austria and Serbia alone. Sazonov was displeased, saying France was trying to hold Russia back at the decisive moment.

note.text: Serbia rejected point 6 as contrary to its constitution and its code of criminal procedure. In explanations on 27 and 28 July, Vienna said the point meant only taking part in the preliminary police investigation.

FR-03P.title: Partial Mobilization
FR-03P.event: On the morning of 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and Belgrade came under bombardment from the early hours of 29 July. The same day Russia announced partial mobilization of the four military districts facing Austria. On the evening of 28 July Madame Caillaux was acquitted.
FR-03P.scene: Because you stayed in Paris, you have received the reports yourself at every stage of the crisis, but by the same token you cannot shift the responsibility onto anyone else. Izvolsky says the German ambassador has told Sazonov that Germany will mobilize too unless Russia halts its military preparations, and he demands a firm answer from France. Joffre reports that Germany is secretly preparing to mobilize, and Paul Cambon in London says Grey has not yet won over his cabinet. The answer to St Petersburg must be settled before dawn.

voices.text: If Russia is late, Germany’s first blow falls entirely on France. Letting our ally see us hesitate is as good as leaving the frontier empty.

voices.who: Paul Cambon (ambassador in London), gist of a telegram
voices.text: British opinion is watching who moves first. If Russia orders general mobilization first, Grey will not carry even his own cabinet.

choices.text: Pledge to fulfill the alliance’s obligations, but urge Russia to avoid any step that would give Germany a pretext to mobilize
choices.why: Keep the alliance, but never forget how London sees it
choices.after: The telegram sent at dawn pledged that France would fulfill its alliance obligations while urging caution. Sazonov sent his thanks, but the Russian general staff kept pressing the Tsar, insisting that partial mobilization alone cannot meet Germany.

choices.text: Answer as Joffre wants, with unconditional support. Whatever measures Russia takes, France goes with her
choices.why: If Russia is slow, Germany’s first blow lands on France
choices.after: Izvolsky, deeply moved, wired home on the spot. With French support confirmed, the Russian general staff pressed even harder for general mobilization.

choices.text: Citing Cambon’s warning, demand that Russia halt mobilization, and say that otherwise France will review its alliance duties
choices.why: Stopping Russia is the price of winning Britain
choices.after: Izvolsky left the Élysée white-faced and went straight to send a long telegram to St Petersburg. Never since the military convention of 1892 had France spoken to its ally like this.

note.text: Russia had already decided on the 'period preparatory to war' at the Krasnoe Selo council on 25 July and put it into effect the next day. Having the French president in Paris changed nothing: Russia had already decided.

FR-01.title: The Tsar’s Table

map.caption: The France left Dunkirk before dawn on 16 July, crossed the North Sea and the Baltic, and reached the roads off Kronstadt on 20 July.

FR-01.event: On the afternoon of 20 July 1914 the French dreadnought France, hurriedly declared complete on 1 July (her formal commissioning came in October), entered the roads off Kronstadt escorted by her sister ship Jean Bart. Nicholas II came out in person aboard the imperial yacht Alexandria to meet you and bring you to Peterhof. By the Julian calendar Russia still used, it was 7 July.
FR-01.scene: The banquet in the Empress Elizabeth hall glitters with gold-braided uniforms and diamonds, and among them your black tailcoat alone looks plain. Even so, the Russian court takes note of the sky-blue sash of the Order of St Andrew across your chest, and of the reply toast you delivered clearly and without notes. That afternoon in St Petersburg, strikes spread through the big factories and workers clashed with the police. Three weeks after the Sarajevo assassination, Vienna has still announced nothing, and the silence is all the more unsettling. Tomorrow morning, when you sit down alone with the Tsar, you must tell him how France sees the dispute between Austria and Serbia.

voices.who: Nicholas II (emperor of Russia), to Paléologue aboard the Alexandria, 20 July
voices.text: It’s all the more important for us to be able to count on England in an emergency. Unless she has gone out of her mind altogether Germany will never attack Russia, France and England combined.
Russia wants to see France’s resolve for itself. If you hesitate even slightly, Monsieur le Président, the Russian court will take it as a sign that France is weak.

The French parliament and public have no wish to go to war over the Balkans. This government came into office having only just saved the three-year service law. We must not be dragged into Russia’s Balkan policy.

choices.text: Share Viviani’s concern: say now that if Russia acts first in the Balkans, the French parliament and public will not follow
choices.why: First of all, keep France clear of an ally’s adventures
choices.after: The Tsar nodded politely, but his expression stiffened. That night Foreign Minister Sazonov carefully asked Paléologue how the French president regarded the alliance.

choices.text: Take Paléologue’s advice: call Serbia’s defense an alliance matter and promise France will side with Russia whatever happens
choices.why: Russia will read the slightest hesitation as weakness
choices.after: The Tsar’s face brightened. The war party at the Russian court took it that France had promised to protect even Serbia, and the words will soon reach Vienna and Berlin.

choices.text: Urge that both nations stand firm with one voice, but keep to talks among all the powers, as in London in 1913
choices.why: Show solidarity, but keep the road to talks open
choices.after: Nicholas II was highly satisfied. According to Paléologue’s memoirs, after their farewell on the night of 23 July the Tsar told him that he and the president had been in complete agreement, and that the harder the situation became, the more solidarity and firmness mattered.

note.text: No official record of the talks between Poincaré and Nicholas II survives. According to Paléologue’s memoirs, Poincaré stressed 'the method that served us so well in 1913': open discussion among all the great powers, without one bloc set against the other. These memoirs, however, were polished and published after the war.

FR-02.place: Winter Palace, St Petersburg: reception for the diplomatic corps
FR-02.title: Ambassador Szápáry
FR-02.clock: About 50 hours until Vienna delivers its ultimatum (you do not know this yet)
FR-02.scene: The ambassadors come before you one by one. Viviani stands on your left, and Paléologue presents his colleagues. With the German ambassador Pourtalès, doyen of the diplomatic corps, you talked only of his family’s French origins and a motor tour through Provence. Next came the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, Count Szápáry, who had spent two months at the bedside of his sick wife and son and returned to his post unexpectedly yesterday. When you asked for news of Serbia he answered coldly that 'the judicial enquiry is proceeding,' and you gently reminded him of two earlier 'inquiries' in which Austria had been embarrassed by forged documents: the Friedjung affair and the Prochaska affair.

voices.text: Monsieur le Président, we cannot suffer a foreign government to allow plots against our sovereignty to be hatched on its territory!
Szápáry’s sudden return means a rupture is near. Vienna sent him back to his post early so that he would share the responsibility for the break.
A head of state must not be seen scolding another country’s ambassador in a foreign capital. Every word you say will go straight to Vienna by telegram.

choices.text: Warn him: 'Serbia has some very warm friends in the Russian people. And Russia has an ally, France.'
choices.why: A firm warning now could make Vienna think again
choices.after: Szápáry bowed and went out without a word. You told Viviani and Paléologue that Austria had a coup de théâtre in store, so Sazonov must be firm and France must back him up (Paléologue’s memoirs). The warning in this choice, however, is Paléologue’s rendering. Poincaré’s own memoirs give a milder version: Serbia had friends in Russia who would no doubt be surprised to see her subjected to harsh measures, and that surprise might be shared in other European countries that were friends of Russia. Szápáry reported to Vienna that the French president’s tone had been threatening.

choices.text: Hint to Szápáry at informal mediation: if Vienna shares its demands in advance, France will work on Belgrade
choices.why: France could head off the crisis by acting as mediator
choices.after: Szápáry avoided an answer, saying he had no instructions, but your offer was reported to Vienna that night. Berchtold may take another look at his text, or he may hurry to act before France can step in.

choices.text: As Viviani advises, say no more about Serbia and end the audience. Whatever an ambassador hears goes straight to Vienna
choices.why: A head of state does not pick quarrels in another’s capital
choices.after: Szápáry withdrew looking relieved. Vienna may conclude that France has no wish to become deeply involved in this affair.

note.text: Vienna moved the delivery of the ultimatum from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m., calculating that by the time the news reached St Petersburg, the French president would already be at sea.

FR-03.place: The battleship France in the Baltic, passing Reval (now Tallinn)
FR-03.title: The President at Sea

map.caption: The original plan was Stockholm on 25 July, Copenhagen on the 27th and Kristiania on the 29th, returning to Dunkirk on the 31st.

FR-03.clock: About 40 hours until Serbia’s deadline (6 p.m., 25 July)
FR-03.event: At 6 p.m. on 23 July the Austro-Hungarian minister, Giesl, handed Belgrade an ultimatum with a 48-hour deadline. That evening you gave a farewell dinner for the Tsar and tsarina on the deck of the France, and at about 11 p.m. you left Kronstadt.

telegram.text: Your instructions urgently passed to Vienna / but Austrian note apparently already delivered Belgrade yesterday 6 p.m. / official text not yet received / terms very harsh / Serbia required to submit by Saturday 6 p.m.

FR-03.scene: The farewell dinner was held on deck beneath the 305mm main guns, and the Russian grand dukes cheered the closing words of your toast. Now the ship is crossing the dark Baltic toward Stockholm, and only broken sentences reach the wireless room. The instruction sent off Reval, to give Vienna 'counsels of moderation,' arrived a step behind the ultimatum. While the head of state and the prime minister are both at sea, the Foreign Ministry in Paris is in the hands of the justice minister, who has almost no diplomatic experience.

voices.text: The two countries have the same ideal of peace in strength, honor and dignity.

voices.who: Viviani (prime minister and foreign minister), on reading Paléologue’s draft press communiqué
voices.text: I don’t much like the last sentence of your note: I think it involves us a little too much in Russia’s Balkan policy . . . Wouldn’t it be better to leave it out?

choices.text: Share Viviani’s concern: instruct Paléologue that Russia must consult Paris before it takes any military measures
choices.why: An ally’s military steps must be checked before they are taken
choices.after: Paléologue passed on the instruction reluctantly. Sazonov was hurt, but the Russian general staff now had to keep one eye on Paris.

choices.text: So that Russia does not feel alone, have Paléologue tell Sazonov plainly that France will stand with Russia to the end
choices.why: Only visible solidarity will make Vienna back down
choices.after: With the president’s instruction in hand, Paléologue urged firmness on Sazonov without reserve, and the Russian council of ministers went into the next day’s meeting sure of French support.

choices.text: In step with Britain, back a longer deadline, and urge Serbia to accept every demand that does not harm its sovereignty
choices.why: Every hour gained gives great-power mediation a chance
choices.after: This choice partly matches what happened. Such advice was in fact driven by Bienvenu-Martin in Paris and by Berthelot of the Foreign Ministry’s political department; you and Viviani, at sea, approved it after the event from telegrams that arrived in fragments. On 25 July Serbia accepted most of the demands, attached reservations to several and rejected point 6, and Giesl left Belgrade that evening.

note.text: France’s acting foreign minister, Jean-Baptiste Bienvenu-Martin, was by office the justice minister and had almost no diplomatic experience. For the first five days of the crisis, French diplomacy was in practice run by Philippe Berthelot of the Foreign Ministry’s political department.

FR-04.place: The France in the Baltic, after leaving Stockholm
FR-04.title: Turn Back?
FR-04.event: On 25 July you met King Gustaf V of Sweden in Stockholm. The same day Serbia delivered its reply just before the deadline, and Giesl left Belgrade on the 6:30 p.m. train. At the Krasnoe Selo council on 25 July, Russia decided on the 'period preparatory to war,' in force from the next day. In St Petersburg, Paléologue had been urging a firm policy on Sazonov since 24 July.
FR-04.scene: Messages come up from the wireless room broken off mid-sentence, and the news is sometimes a day old when it arrives. A telegram from Paris received overnight says the ministers left behind are unanimous in wanting you back, and that the newspapers have begun to blame the president for continuing the tour. Viviani is sleeping badly and his nerves are on edge. On the original schedule you would call at Copenhagen on 27 July and Kristiania (now Oslo) on the 29th, landing at Dunkirk only on the 31st. Break off the tour suddenly and Europe will take it that the French president expects war; stay at sea and France faces the crisis without its leaders. Yet the front pages of the Paris papers are still given over to the Caillaux trial.

voices.text: We cannot stay at sea any longer. The Foreign Ministry in Paris is in the hands of the justice minister, and the papers are starting to ask where the government is.

voices.who: Paléologue (ambassador to Russia), gist of a telegram
voices.text: While you and the prime minister are at sea, I am making judgments without instructions. It is an unprecedented position for an ambassador, and the responsibility is heavy.

choices.text: As the ministers in Paris ask, cancel the visits to Copenhagen and Kristiania and head straight back to Dunkirk
choices.why: A government cannot be absent in the middle of a crisis
choices.after: On the morning of 27 July you and Viviani decided to cut the tour short and sent telegrams of apology to the kings of Denmark and Norway. The France crossed the North Sea and entered Dunkirk on the morning of 29 July. In St Petersburg, meanwhile, Paléologue had in effect been conferring with the Russians on his own judgment.

choices.text: Call at Copenhagen and Kristiania as planned. Cut the schedule and rush home, and Europe will read it as a sign war is near
choices.why: A show of haste would only feed the crisis
choices.after: The France held her course for Copenhagen. The Danish court had prepared a lavish welcome, but the Paris papers have begun to ask where the president is.

note.text: Henriette Caillaux, wife of the former prime minister Joseph Caillaux, shot dead Gaston Calmette, editor of Le Figaro, on 16 March 1914 after his paper had campaigned against her husband. Her trial opened on 20 July, absorbed the attention of Paris, and ended in acquittal on 28 July.

pressure.title: The Courtroom and the Cipher
pressure.text: While you are at sea, Madame Caillaux’s trial goes on in Paris, and the newspapers' attention is fixed on it. Right after the decrypted German telegrams exposed the secret negotiations of Caillaux’s side in 1911, Germany changed its diplomatic codes, and according to your memoirs the French Foreign Ministry could no longer read German diplomatic ciphers from the end of that year. On 21 July, the second day of the trial, a journalist from Le Figaro testified that Calmette had shown him documents proving Caillaux’s treason, and Caillaux retorted that he would bring out whatever he needed to defend himself. The ministers left in Paris drafted a statement after an all-night meeting, and on 22 July it was announced in court that the so-called 'green documents' were nothing but false copies of documents that had never existed. The longer you stay at sea, the more the Paris papers will make of the government’s absence.

FR-04B.place: The France in the Kattegat, bound from Copenhagen for Kristiania
FR-04B.title: Mobilization by Wireless

telegram.text: Austria today declared war on Serbia / Russia hastening military preparations / Germany warns it will mobilize if Russia does

FR-04B.scene: The banquet in Denmark ended in haste. At sea, telegrams arrive half a day late, and the acting foreign minister in Paris is left to guess at your wishes. In St Petersburg, Paléologue hears the Russian generals' decisions at close quarters, but his reports are brief and late. All you can do now is send a few lines by telegram from the ship.

voices.text: If Russia orders general mobilization first, Britain will not take France’s side. We must tell them not to give Germany a pretext.

voices.who: Adolphe Messimy (war minister), gist of a telegram
voices.text: Reports keep coming that Germany is secretly preparing to mobilize. Give me authority to move the frontier covering troops before you return.

choices.text: As Viviani says, send an instruction from the ship not to give Germany a pretext to mobilize, and hurry home
choices.why: Urge the ally to caution, however late the hour
choices.after: The instruction reached St Petersburg a day late. The France gave up the Kristiania visit and entered Dunkirk on the morning of 30 July.

choices.text: As Messimy requests, leave the frontier to him and Russia to Paléologue, and hurry home
choices.why: Men on the spot with authority act faster than orders sent from afar
choices.after: Paléologue read the president’s delegation as blanket support for Russia. The France gave up the Kristiania visit and entered Dunkirk on the morning of 30 July.

note.text: In 1914 wireless reception varied greatly with distance and weather, and decoding a coded telegram and writing it out again took hours. Poincaré’s party did in fact spend most of 24 to 28 July at sea (apart from the call at Stockholm on 25 and 26 July), receiving only fragments of news.

FR-05.title: Give Them No Pretext
FR-05.event: On the morning of 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and Belgrade came under bombardment from the early hours of 29 July. On the evening of that same 28 July the Paris assize court acquitted Madame Caillaux. On 29 July Russia announced partial mobilization of the four military districts facing Austria (Odessa, Kiev, Moscow and Kazan).
FR-05.scene: Landing at Dunkirk on the morning of 29 July, you came by train to the Gare du Nord and were cheered by crowds lining the way from the station to the Élysée. Tonight, shortly before 2 a.m. and just after you have gone to bed, Viviani hurries to the Élysée with a telegram from Sazonov that the Russian embassy has just delivered. The German ambassador has told Sazonov that Germany will mobilize too unless Russia halts its military preparations. Russia says it has no choice but to speed up its arming, regards war as imminent, and counts on the help of its ally France. The reply to St Petersburg must be settled before dawn.

voices.text: If Russia slows its mobilization, Germany turns its whole strength on France. Holding back our ally at a moment like this is no different from leaving the French frontier empty.
London is watching to see who moves first. If Russia orders general mobilization first, Grey will not carry even his own cabinet.

choices.text: To keep Britain, Russia must stop. Demand a halt to mobilization, and say France will review its alliance duties if refused
choices.why: If Russia moves first, France loses Britain
choices.after: Izvolsky turned white. Never since the military convention of 1892 had France spoken to its ally like this.

choices.text: As Messimy says, raise no objection to Russia’s military steps. Answer that whatever Russia does, France goes with her
choices.why: Hold the ally back, and the frontier is in danger at once
choices.after: Izvolsky, deeply moved, wired home on the spot. With French support confirmed, the Russian general staff pressed even harder for general mobilization.

choices.text: Pledge to 'fulfil all the obligations' of the alliance, but urge Sazonov to avoid for now any step that hands Germany a pretext
choices.why: France can keep the alliance without losing Britain
choices.after: Viviani’s telegram, sent at 7 a.m., declared that 'France is resolved to fulfil all the obligations of her alliance' while urging caution. Sazonov replied that the general staff had suspended its precautionary measures overnight, but that afternoon Nicholas II approved general mobilization again, and Paléologue informed Paris only on 31 July.

note.text: The Franco-Russian military convention of 1892 provided that if Russia were attacked by Germany, or by Austria supported by Germany, France would use all her available forces against Germany. It also provided that if any member of the Triple Alliance mobilized, both countries would mobilize at once and simultaneously.

FR-05B.place: The Élysée Palace in Paris and the Foreign Ministry in St Petersburg
FR-05B.title: The Day the Alliance Wavered
FR-05B.scene: When the French demand reached him, Sazonov raised his voice at Paléologue: if Russia backed down again, as in the Bosnian crisis of 1909, its standing in the Slav world would be finished. The Russian general staff presses the Tsar, insisting that partial mobilization alone cannot meet Germany, and Nicholas II prays and puts off his decision. In Paris, Izvolsky has begun to call your decision 'a betrayal of the alliance.'

voices.who: Nikolai Basily (deputy director of the chancellery, Russian Foreign Ministry), to Paléologue on the night of 29 July
voices.text: From the technical point of view a partial mobilization could be carried out only at the price of dislocating the entire machinery of general mobilization.

voices.who: Joseph Joffre (chief of the general staff)
voices.text: If Russia is late, Germany’s first blow falls entirely on France. France can hold only if Russia moves fast in the east.

choices.text: Hold firm. Promise that if Russia stops at partial mobilization, France will stay at her side at the conference table to the end
choices.why: Shield a Russia that halts, and the alliance survives
choices.after: On the strength of France’s word, Nicholas II overruled his generals. With Russia stopping at partial mobilization of thirteen corps on the Austrian front, Berlin, for the first time, has to think again.

choices.text: Withdraw the demand and return to the earlier alliance pledge. On the technical side of mobilization, defer to the Russian staff
choices.why: A broken alliance is more dangerous than war
choices.after: Izvolsky was relieved, but Russia’s leaders did not forget that France had hesitated once. That afternoon Nicholas II approved general mobilization again.

note.text: The Russian general staff had prepared no separate plan for partial mobilization. The Russian generals' strongest argument was therefore that partial mobilization would tangle the railway timetables for general mobilization.

FR-06.title: Ten Kilometers

map.caption: From 30 July, French covering troops from Luxembourg to the Vosges were not allowed past a line set back ten kilometers from the frontier.

FR-06.scene: A report comes in that Germany has posted covering troops a few hundred meters from the frontier all the way from Luxembourg to the Vosges. Joffre, chief of the general staff, demands that the French covering troops also go to their battle positions. Plan XVII, drawn up on the assumption of an offensive, places the covering troops as close to the frontier as possible. But in London Grey’s cabinet has promised nothing yet, and British opinion is watching to see who crosses a frontier first.

voices.text: Leaving ten kilometers empty means giving up heights, villages and railway junctions without a fight. In this war, every day of delay costs us ground.

voices.who: Viviani (prime minister and foreign minister), instructions to the ambassador in London
voices.text: By leaving a strip of territory undefended against sudden aggression of the enemy, the Government of the Republic hopes to prove that France does not bear, any more than Russia, the responsibility for the attack.

choices.text: As Joffre demands, push the covering troops right up to the frontier in battle positions and seize the heights and rail junctions
choices.why: The ground held in the first days decides the whole war
choices.after: Joffre was satisfied and the frontier villages cheered. But German newspapers reported French troops pressed up against the border, and the non-interventionist ministers in London carried those articles into the cabinet room.

choices.text: Keep even the covering troops where they are until mobilization is ordered. London must never hear that France moved first
choices.why: Any military step narrows the room left for diplomacy
choices.after: Joffre hinted that he would resign, saying he could not answer for the consequences. People in the frontier districts grew anxious that no troops were coming.

choices.text: Deploy the covering troops but bar them from crossing a line ten kilometers back from the frontier, and tell London at once
choices.why: Winning Britain’s trust is worth a little ground
choices.after: War Minister Messimy issued the order, and Viviani immediately instructed Cambon in London to inform Grey. Joffre made no secret of his displeasure. The ten-kilometer line was lifted only after 2 p.m. on 2 August, once German patrols had crossed the frontier, and even then with the proviso that the frontier itself must not be crossed.

note.text: The letters Grey and Cambon exchanged in November 1912 stated that consultation between the two countries' military and naval experts 'does not restrict the freedom of either Government.' Britain had no obligation to fight alongside France; all France could count on was British opinion.

FR-06H.title: Russia Halts
FR-06H.scene: With Russia stopping at partial mobilization, Berlin’s thinking begins to shift. Jules Cambon, ambassador in Berlin and Paul Cambon’s younger brother, reports that Bethmann Hollweg is pressing Vienna to 'halt in Belgrade.' But Moltke is pressing the kaiser, arguing that Russia’s partial mobilization alone puts Germany in danger. Austrian river monitors are still shelling Belgrade.

voices.who: Paul Cambon (ambassador in London), gist of a telegram
voices.text: Grey has revived four-power mediation. If France takes the lead, the British cabinet may move too.
The German army is still on the frontier, and the longer the talks go on, the closer Germany comes to finishing its preparations. France cannot be the only one sitting idle.

choices.text: On Paul Cambon’s advice, publicly back Grey’s four-power mediation and name Cambon France’s delegate to a conference in London
choices.why: The method of 1913 can keep the peace once again
choices.after: In early August the ambassadors of Britain, France, Germany and Italy sat down together again at the Foreign Office in London, exactly as they had in 1913 to settle the Balkan wars.

choices.text: Negotiate directly with Berlin through Jules Cambon: accept a temporary occupation of Belgrade in return for guaranteed talks
choices.why: A direct bargain with Berlin is the quicker road to peace
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg showed interest, but Russian newspapers wrote that France was making a back-room deal with Germany.

choices.text: Soothe Russia with the promise of a new railway loan, and leave the negotiations with Austria in Grey’s hands
choices.why: Soothe the ally’s wounded pride with money first
choices.after: The Russian finance ministry was pleased, and Russian bonds edged up on the Paris Bourse.

note.text: In 1913 France agreed to lend Russia large sums every year on condition that Russia build strategic railways toward its western frontier. The savings of small French investors were thus tied directly to the speed of Russian mobilization.

FR-07H.title: The Price of Belgrade
FR-07H.scene: The ambassadors of the great powers have gathered again in Grey’s room. Austria says it will occupy Belgrade until Serbia keeps the promises demanded in the ultimatum; Russia demands immediate withdrawal. The Serbian government waits in Niš for the outcome. Which side the French delegate, Paul Cambon, takes will decide where the conference goes.

voices.text: Russia has already stepped back once. As long as Austrian troops remain in Belgrade, Russian opinion will remember this peace as a humiliation.
There must be a way to save both Austria’s face and Serbia’s sovereignty. If either side wins outright, the next crisis will not be long in coming.

choices.text: As Izvolsky demands, side with Russia and call for the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Austrian troops
choices.why: Stepping back again would cost France Russia’s trust
choices.after: The conference went round in circles for weeks. Austria did not leave Belgrade, and Russia came to believe in France’s loyalty once more.

choices.text: Propose that an international commission supervise Serbia’s inquiry while Austrian troops withdraw in stages
choices.why: Saving face on both sides is what prevents the next crisis
choices.after: Grey accepted the plan, and Italy and Germany followed. By autumn the Austrian troops had pulled back across the Sava.

choices.text: Together with Britain, accept Austria’s occupation of Belgrade for a fixed period and bring the conference to a quick close
choices.why: A quick peace beats months of drawn-out talks
choices.after: The conference ended quickly, but Serbia had to negotiate with its capital in enemy hands. In St Petersburg people say France has abandoned Russia once again.

note.text: The London conference of ambassadors, held from December 1912 to August 1913, kept the Balkan wars from turning into a war among the great powers. At that time Germany restrained Austria, and Britain led the conference together with Germany.

FR-07H2.title: A Letter from the Tsar
FR-07H2.scene: Since the London conference ended, the mood in St Petersburg has been cold. Russia has stepped back for the second time since the Bosnian crisis of 1909, and amid the humiliation, conservatives such as Durnovo, who in February 1914 sent the Tsar a memorandum urging him to avoid war with Germany, are beginning to talk of an understanding with Berlin. A personal letter from Nicholas II arrives at the Élysée: Russia stepped back because it trusted France’s word, and now France should show what the alliance is worth.

voices.who: Paléologue (ambassador to Russia), gist of a telegram
voices.text: Around the Tsar people are saying that at the decisive moment France left Russia standing alone. Without a firm commitment, the alliance will cool.
Every new commitment narrows the choices open to France in the next crisis. Nor will parliament approve commitments made for the sake of the Balkans.

choices.text: As Paléologue proposes, increase the Russian railway loans and have both countries declare jointly that the alliance is unchanged
choices.why: Money and railways hold an alliance together better than words
choices.after: The Tsar sent a letter of thanks, and a new Russian loan was floated on the Paris Bourse. Berlin concluded that the alliance had come out of the crisis stronger, and grew more wary.

choices.text: Promise in secret to back Russia on the question of the Turkish Straits as well, as Sazonov has long wished
choices.why: Only a large promise will revive a cooling alliance
choices.after: Sazonov was delighted, but the promise risked collisions with both Britain and the Ottoman Empire. Rumors of the secret pledge soon reached the German embassy in Constantinople.

choices.text: As Viviani says, make clear the alliance is defensive, and propose regular great-power consultation that includes Britain
choices.why: New promises would narrow France’s choices in the next crisis
choices.after: Grey welcomed the proposal, and regular consultations on the model of the London conference came under discussion. St Petersburg was hurt, feeling that France was hiding the alliance behind an international conference.

note.text: In February 1914 the former interior minister Pyotr Durnovo warned Nicholas II in a memorandum that Russia had almost nothing to gain from a war with Germany, that defeat would make social revolution unavoidable, and that the war must therefore be avoided.

FR-08H.title: Paying for Peace
FR-08H.scene: Peace has been kept, but the nationalist papers attack the president for abandoning Russia and forgetting Alsace-Lorraine for good. The Socialists welcome the decision that kept the peace and demand that the three-year service law be cut back to two years, while Joseph Caillaux, husband of the acquitted Madame Caillaux, returns to the political stage as the champion of reconciliation with Germany. In St Petersburg, Russia’s 'Great Programme' of rearmament, due to be completed in 1917, goes on.

voices.text: Germany has completed its army increases of 1913. If we abandon the three-year law, France will not survive the first month of the next crisis.
What this summer showed is that negotiation, not armaments, kept the peace. There is no reason to keep young men in barracks for three years.

choices.text: As Joffre says, keep the three-year service law and increase the Russian railway loans to shore up the alliance
choices.why: Only a balance of power can keep the peace
choices.after: With French money, Russia built railways and shortened its mobilization time. The German general staff grows ever more convinced that time is not on Germany’s side.

choices.text: Try the path Caillaux and the Socialists urge, and propose to Germany that both sides slow the arms race
choices.why: The lesson of this summer is negotiation, not armaments
choices.after: Berlin’s response was lukewarm, but the conversation did not break off. St Petersburg suspected Paris of a change of heart.

choices.text: Formally propose to Britain that the Triple Entente become a military alliance. In the next crisis, France will not wait on London
choices.why: Only a clear British commitment can prevent the next crisis
choices.after: Grey politely asked for time. Most of the British Liberal Party was still reluctant to be bound to continental alliances.

note.text: At the Winter Palace on 21 July 1914, Poincaré told the British ambassador, Buchanan, that Britain would eventually realize the need to turn the Triple Entente into a Triple Alliance.

FR-07.place: Café du Croissant, rue Montmartre, Paris, and the Élysée Palace
FR-07.title: Jaurès
FR-07.event: At midday on 31 July Germany proclaimed a 'state of imminent danger of war.' At 7 p.m. the German ambassador, Schoen, called on Viviani to ask what attitude France would take in a war between Russia and Germany, and said he would come back for the answer at 1 p.m. the next day. Paléologue’s telegram reporting Russia’s general mobilization reached Paris only late that day, and the personal letter you had written to King George V of Britain was delivered to the king that evening.

telegram.text: Café du Croissant, rue Montmartre / Deputy Jaurès shot through window, dead / assailant Raoul Villain arrested at scene

FR-07.scene: Two days ago the Socialist leader Jean Jaurès came back from the meeting of the International Socialist Bureau in Brussels, where he had spoken out against war. This evening too he went to the Foreign Ministry to press the government on its intentions; afterward, at a late supper with colleagues from L’Humanité, he was shot through the window. The killer was a 28-year-old nationalist who saw Jaurès, an opponent of the three-year law, as a traitor. Will there be riots in the working-class districts? Will the unions answer a mobilization order with a general strike? No one knows what Paris will look like tomorrow morning.

voices.text: The antiwar activists on the Carnet B list must be picked up tonight. Mobilization depends on the railways, and a single strike can stop the railways.
The unions are signaling that they will answer the call-up. Start arresting people tonight and we turn Jaurès’s comrades into enemies.

choices.text: Send condolences to Jaurès’s widow and appeal for unity. As Malvy advises, make no arrests from the Carnet B list
choices.why: Mobilization succeeds only if the workers are not made enemies
choices.after: The next day the government decided not to apply Carnet B. The CGT and the Socialist Party answered the mobilization, and at Jaurès’s funeral on 4 August Léon Jouhaux, general secretary of the CGT, spoke of defending the nation. The same day, in your message to parliament, you named this spirit the 'sacred union.'

choices.text: Faced with Jaurès’s death, issue a last appeal for peace and ask the German Social Democrats to answer it with the same appeal
choices.why: The workers of both nations might yet hold back their governments
choices.after: The appeal was printed in the Social Democratic press in Berlin, but the German government was already on the brink of mobilizing. Russia asks what the French president is waiting for.

choices.text: As the prefecture demands, round up the Carnet B activists tonight to forestall rail strikes and sabotage of mobilization
choices.why: A single strike could stop the entire mobilization
choices.after: The activists on the list were taken away during the night. Troops were posted in the working-class districts, and the Socialist press wrote that the government is exploiting Jaurès’s death.

note.text: The killer, Raoul Villain, was acquitted at his trial in March 1919, after the war. Jaurès’s remains were moved to the Panthéon in 1924.

pressure.title: The Death of a Rival
pressure.text: Jaurès, who led the campaign against the three-year service law, was your longtime political adversary. In mid-July an extraordinary congress of the Socialist Party in Paris voted, by 1,690 to 1,174, that a workers' general strike organized simultaneously in several countries was a particularly effective means of preventing war. The Prefecture of Police’s Carnet B list was drawn up precisely in readiness for such a general strike and for obstruction of mobilization. Yet at the Brussels meeting on 29 July Jaurès had not given up hope that the governments would draw back at the last moment.

FR-08.title: The Price of Neutrality
FR-08.clock: Ambassador Schoen’s deadline for a reply: 1 p.m., 1 August
FR-08.scene: The German ambassador, Wilhelm von Schoen, comes to the Quai d’Orsay again. Last night he asked Viviani for help should he have to leave Paris, and even raised the matter of his passports. His bag holds one more instruction he has not yet produced: if France declares neutrality, it is to hand over the frontier fortresses of Toul and Verdun as a pledge, to be returned when the war with Russia is over. Until the Agadir crisis of 1911 the French Foreign Ministry had been reading deciphered German diplomatic telegrams, but it lost that window when Germany changed its codes at the end of that year. Poincaré himself wrote in his memoirs that Schoen’s 1914 telegrams were first deciphered only during the war, under the Clemenceau government, and that this final section, in a more complex cipher, was even then only partly broken. There is no evidence that on this day the French government knew of the demand in advance.

voices.who: Viviani (prime minister and foreign minister), telegram to St Petersburg on the night of 31 July
voices.text: The Government of the Republic need not indeed give any account of her intentions except to her ally.

voices.who: Radical deputies of the peace camp
voices.text: France has no obligation to fight for Serbia. The military convention comes into play when Germany attacks Russia, and Germany has not yet declared war on Russia.

choices.text: Demand that Schoen reveal every instruction in his bag, and publish this exchange in which Germany pressed for neutrality
choices.why: Exposing German pressure will win France the moral case
choices.after: Schoen evaded the question and withdrew stiffly, but when Viviani published the exchange, newspapers around the world put Germany’s pressure on France to stay neutral on their front pages. The non-interventionists in London were left with nothing to say, though the demand for Toul and Verdun stayed in Schoen’s bag and came to light only after the war.

choices.text: Answer only that 'France will do what her interests dictate,' sidestep the neutrality question, and give Germany no commitment
choices.why: The safest course is to commit France to nothing at all
choices.after: At 1:05 p.m. Schoen reported to Berlin that 'France would do that which her interests dictated' (German White Book). The instruction demanding Toul and Verdun was to be produced only if France declared neutrality, so it was never delivered. That evening Germany declared war on Russia.

choices.text: As the Radical peace camp urges, declare neutrality. Until Germany declares war on Russia, do not invoke the military convention
choices.why: France has no reason to fight before the convention applies
choices.after: Schoen, startled, was speechless for a moment, then took the second instruction from his bag.

note.text: The demand for Toul and Verdun was in the final section of a secret instruction Bethmann Hollweg sent Schoen on 31 July, to be delivered only if France declared neutrality. France did not declare neutrality, so the demand was never actually made.

FR-08N.title: Toul and Verdun

map.caption: Toul and Verdun, which Germany meant to demand as a pledge of French neutrality, were the two pillars of France’s eastern fortress line.

FR-08N.scene: Ambassador Schoen reads out the second instruction: as a pledge of neutrality, France must hand the fortresses of Toul and Verdun over to the German army. Verdun is the fortress city on the Meuse little more than 50 kilometers from your hometown of Bar-le-Duc, and Toul is the other fortress of the eastern defense line, guarding the Moselle. At the same hour in London, the German ambassador, Lichnowsky, is discussing with the British the idea that if France stays neutral, Germany might not attack her.

voices.text: Toul and Verdun are the core of the eastern frontier defenses. Give up the two fortresses and France must leave its frontier open and rely on German goodwill.

voices.who: Paul Cambon (ambassador in London), gist of a telegram
voices.text: Britain is considering a plan to guarantee French neutrality. But no country will ever again trust a promise signed by a France that abandoned Russia.

choices.text: As Joffre says, not one fortress can be handed over. Withdraw the neutrality declaration and order general mobilization at once
choices.why: Neutrality paid for with the fortresses is surrender
choices.after: Schoen withdrew stiffly. Hours late, the general mobilization order went up on the walls of every town hall in the country. Russia was relieved, but the record will show that France spoke of neutrality for half a day.

choices.text: Refuse the fortresses, but counter with armed neutrality guaranteed by Britain, on the lines Lichnowsky raised in London
choices.why: A British guarantee would keep France safe without fighting
choices.after: In Berlin, Wilhelm II welcomed the offer, saying the whole army could then be turned east, and Moltke despaired. German troop trains began to change direction.

note.text: From 1874 France built a fortress line designed by General Séré de Rivières, linking Verdun, Toul, Épinal and Belfort. Germany’s war plan ran through Belgium precisely so as not to strike this line head-on.

FR-08N2.title: Guaranteed Neutrality
FR-08N2.scene: Britain has promised to guarantee French neutrality as long as Germany does not attack France, and the German army is turning its troop trains east. In St Petersburg Sazonov calls the French decision a 'betrayal,' and Izvolsky is preparing to leave Paris. On the Place de la Concorde, in front of the statue of Strasbourg draped in black since 1871, young nationalists gather and shout 'Alsace-Lorraine!'

voices.text: A peace bought by abandoning Russia is not peace but a postponed surrender. Once Germany has finished in the east, it will come back west.
There is no reason for hundreds of thousands of young Frenchmen to die for the Slavs of the Balkans. Armed neutrality will protect France.

choices.text: Hold to armed neutrality with mobilization in place, and keep the alliance alive by sending Russia loans and munitions
choices.why: France can help its ally without fighting
choices.after: The French army stood watch on the frontier, weapons in hand. Only the French money and shells sent to Russia kept the alliance barely alive.

choices.text: As Caillaux’s followers urge, stand down the mobilization, suspend the military convention with Russia, and choose full neutrality
choices.why: The lives of young Frenchmen weigh more than the alliance
choices.after: The Franco-Russian alliance that had stood since 1894 was in effect over. France’s soldiers went home, and Europe no longer trusts France.

choices.text: Heeding Clemenceau’s warning, abandon neutrality and order general mobilization once German troops enter Luxembourg
choices.why: Once Germany finishes in the east, it will turn west
choices.after: At the news that the German 16th Division had seized Luxembourg’s railways, the case for neutrality collapsed within a day. Because mobilization was ordered late, the first days on the frontier will be all the more dangerous.

note.text: The statue of Strasbourg on the Place de la Concorde was draped in black crepe and funeral wreaths after Alsace-Lorraine was lost in 1871; the mourning was removed only in November 1918.

FR-09.title: Mobilization Is Not War
FR-09.clock: The 12-hour deadline Germany gave Russia has already passed
FR-09.scene: Yesterday Joffre submitted a memorandum warning that every 24-hour delay in calling up the reservists would push the concentration line back and give up that much territory from the outset. He reckoned it at 15 to 25 kilometers a day. At 9 a.m. today he came to the Élysée with Messimy and said he could not take responsibility if mobilization was delayed, and the cabinet approved sending the mobilization telegrams at 4 p.m. Now Messimy stands before you with the mobilization order, waiting for your signature. Germany entered its 'state of imminent danger of war' yesterday, and reports keep coming of troop trains lined up at every station across the border. Once you sign, posters headed 'General Mobilization' and marked with the tricolor will go up at every town hall in France, and with 2 August as the first day, more than three million men will put on uniform.

voices.text: Every day of delay costs fifteen to twenty-five kilometers. If the government does not decide, I cannot bear this responsibility.

voices.who: Paul Cambon (ambassador in London), gist of a telegram
voices.text: The British cabinet is still divided. The sight of France rushing to the frontier first would hand the non-interventionists their pretext. Even if you mobilize, please keep to the line set back from the frontier.

choices.text: Sign the general mobilization order Messimy has brought, but with Britain in mind keep the ten-kilometer line in force
choices.why: Mobilize quickly, but keep the moral case intact to the end
choices.after: The mobilization telegrams went out across the country at about 4 p.m., and Germany’s general mobilization order came at almost the same moment (5 p.m. Berlin time). Many accounts record that, especially in the countryside, people met the posters less with cheers than with silence and resignation.

choices.text: Hold the mobilization telegrams for 24 hours and wait for final answers from London and Berlin. Do not be the first to mobilize
choices.why: One more day could set diplomacy moving again
choices.after: Joffre came back to the Élysée with his resignation in hand. With the order a day late, France’s concentration line now falls behind the plan.

choices.text: As Joffre demands, lift the ten-kilometer limit along with general mobilization and send the covering troops up to the frontier
choices.why: There is no reason to give up ground in a fight already begun
choices.after: Joffre issued the order at once. The next morning German newspapers reported French troops massing on the frontier.

note.text: The proclamation to the nation that you and every minister signed that day said: 'Mobilization is not war. In present circumstances it appears, on the contrary, to be the best means of securing peace with honor.'

FR-09a.place: The president’s study, Élysée Palace, Paris
FR-09a.title: What Will France Do?
FR-09a.event: On the evening of 1 August (about 7 p.m. Russian time), the German ambassador, Pourtalès, handed Sazonov the declaration of war in St Petersburg. France’s first day of mobilization begins a few hours later, on 2 August.
FR-09a.scene: The officer on duty brings word that the Russian ambassador, Izvolsky, urgently asks to see you. When you come down from your private apartments to the study, Izvolsky is standing there, his face distorted, and he announces in a trembling voice that Germany has declared war on Russia. Nothing has come yet from Paléologue in St Petersburg. Germany has not yet declared war on France, and the British cabinet is still putting off its decision.

voices.text: At so tragic an hour, Monsieur le Président, I felt I must turn to the head of the allied State and put a question to him: what is France going to do?
In the grief that grips me, it is hardly of Russia, I confess, that I am thinking; it is above all of France under threat.

choices.text: Wait for London’s answer: tell him France can promise nothing until the British cabinet has made up its mind
choices.why: A war without Britain is more than France can bear
choices.after: Izvolsky bowed his head in silence and reported to St Petersburg that night that France was hiding behind Britain. The Russian general staff, which knew the terms of the 1892 military convention well, was shocked by France’s hesitation.

choices.text: Give Izvolsky the promise he wants on the spot: France will not wait for Germany but will itself declare war tomorrow
choices.why: The ally’s anxiety must be relieved at once
choices.after: Izvolsky, deeply moved, wired home immediately. But Cambon in London sent a telegram warning that a French declaration of war would hand Britain’s non-interventionists their best pretext.

choices.text: Say France will honor the alliance, but push on with mobilization and wait a few days for Germany to declare war first
choices.why: Leaving the declaration to Germany will bring Britain in
choices.after: You told him that the government alone was entitled to answer his question, and summoned the ministers at once. The cabinet unanimously approved your answer, and Viviani told Izvolsky, who was waiting in the officers' anteroom, that France would keep its word but that it was better to decide nothing for a few days. Izvolsky, who had hoped for an immediate public declaration, left looking downcast.

note.text: Under the constitution the president could not make diplomatic commitments on his own, which is why Poincaré first told Izvolsky that the government alone was entitled to answer. Paléologue’s telegram reporting the German declaration of war left St Petersburg at 12:19 a.m. on 2 August and reached Paris only at 2 p.m. that day.

pressure.title: The Ally’s Question
pressure.text: The military convention of 1892 provided that if Germany attacked Russia, France would fight Germany with all its forces, but it did not say when France had to declare war. If France declared war first, it would hand the non-interventionists in the British cabinet the very pretext they most wanted. Nor has any reply yet come to the personal letter you sent King George V of Britain on 31 July. Tonight you must buy time, caught between loyalty to the alliance and the need to win over Britain.

FR-10.place: The Foreign Office in London and the Élysée Palace in Paris
FR-10.title: A Question of Honor
FR-10.event: On the evening of 1 August Germany declared war on Russia. On the morning of 2 August German troops entered neutral Luxembourg, and that same morning, at the French frontier village of Joncherey, Corporal Jules-André Peugeot was shot dead in an encounter with a German patrol. He was the first French soldier killed in the war of 1914.
FR-10.scene: Paul Cambon, the ambassador in London, is 71. He has been there since 1898, yet he will not hold a conversation in English. On 31 July, as he left Grey’s room, the permanent under-secretary, Nicolson, tried to comfort him by saying the cabinet would meet again the next day. But on 1 August he received the same answer, and he is said to have come out pale and told Nicolson that Britain was going to abandon France. Since 1912, in line with naval talks with Britain, the French fleet has been concentrated in the Mediterranean, leaving the northern coasts on the Channel and the Atlantic practically bare. This morning the British cabinet meets again.

voices.who: Sir Edward Grey (British foreign secretary), to Cambon on 31 July (Grey’s own record)
voices.text: We could not give any pledge at the present time. Though we should have to put our policy before Parliament, we could not pledge Parliament in advance.

France sent its fleet to the Mediterranean trusting its understanding with Britain, and left its northern coast bare in return. If Britain washes its hands of us now, it is no longer a question of policy but of honor.

choices.text: Pressure London by announcing that unless Britain publicly pledges to fight, France will reconsider the Triple Entente
choices.why: Public pressure will move a hesitant cabinet
choices.after: Britain’s non-interventionist ministers bristled at the public pressure, and Liberal papers wrote that France was trying to drag Britain into the war. Grey found himself more isolated in the cabinet.

choices.text: Citing the 1912 letters and the fleet massed in the Mediterranean, keep pleading Britain’s moral duty to guard the north coast
choices.why: Britain’s sense of good faith will move it, promise or no promise
choices.after: After the cabinet, Grey handed Cambon a memorandum: if the German fleet came into the Channel or through the North Sea to undertake hostile operations against French coasts or shipping, the British fleet would give all the protection in its power. John Burns, who opposed the decision, resigned, and John Morley followed him. France had already replied on 31 July to Grey’s inquiry that it would respect Belgian neutrality.

choices.text: Do not lead with moral obligation. Put the question of Belgian neutrality first, so that Grey can win over his cabinet
choices.why: Britain moves only for its own interests
choices.after: Cambon did not raise the naval question. The British cabinet put off its decision until German troops crossed the Belgian frontier, and until then the bare northern coast remained France’s weak point.

note.text: Explaining the naval assurance of 2 August to the British ambassador in Paris, Grey wrote that 'it was essential to the French Government, whose fleet had long been concentrated in the Mediterranean, to know how to make their dispositions with their north coast entirely undefended.'

FR-10a.title: The Goeben and the Navy Minister

map.caption: On the morning of 3 August Rome announced its neutrality and Brussels its rejection of the German ultimatum, while London had still not decided to enter the war.

FR-10a.clock: About 10 hours until Germany declares war at 6:45 p.m. (you do not know this yet)
FR-10a.event: At 7 p.m. on 2 August the German minister in Brussels handed the Belgian government an ultimatum. On the false pretext that French troops meant to advance on the Meuse by way of Namur, it demanded passage for the German army. The Belgian king and his ministers met through the night and unanimously refused. At 9 a.m. on 3 August the Italian chargé d’affaires, Prince Ruspoli, called on Viviani to give formal notice of Italy’s neutrality.
FR-10a.scene: At 11 o’clock last night you had to summon Navy Minister Gauthier to the Élysée together with the chief of the naval staff, because he had completely forgotten the cabinet’s order to close the Strait of Dover with torpedo boats and submarines. Then Gauthier swung the other way and sent a letter proposing that Admiral Lapeyrère’s fleet attack the German battlecruiser Goeben and the light cruiser Breslau before war had even been declared. The two ships have coaled at a port in southern Italy and are heading down into the western Mediterranean, the very waters the transports must cross to bring the XIX Corps from Algeria to France. Messimy, who arrived at the Élysée early this morning, berated Gauthier as incompetent, and Gauthier retorted that he would send him his seconds.

voices.text: We must strike the Goeben before she falls on the transports. If we wait for a declaration of war, we will lose the Algerian troops at sea.

voices.who: Joffre (chief of the general staff), order to the army commanders at 5:30 p.m. on 2 August (agreed with Viviani)
voices.text: For national reasons of a moral order and for compelling reasons of a diplomatic order, it is indispensable to leave to the Germans the entire responsibility for hostilities.

choices.text: Forbid any attack on the Goeben before war is declared, and accept the resignation of Gauthier, worn out by his clash with Messimy
choices.why: What matters most is not to be the one who fires first
choices.after: When you stepped in, the two ministers' quarrel ended in tears and an embrace, and Gauthier, his health broken, resigned. Victor Augagneur took over the navy, and Viviani handed the Foreign Ministry to Gaston Doumergue. You had wanted a broader government of national union, but Viviani, who tried to bring in Briand and Delcassé, ran into opposition on the left and gave up the idea. Before dawn the next day the Goeben and the Breslau shelled Bône and Philippeville in Algeria and vanished; the Algerian divisions later crossed the sea safely under escort.

choices.text: Trust the Italian neutrality Prince Ruspoli has announced, and shift the troops on the Alpine frontier to the northeast at once
choices.why: Italy’s word lets France gather its main strength
choices.after: Italian neutrality did in fact allow France to move the forces it had kept on the Alpine side to the northeast. It came somewhat later, though: the 44th Division, formed near Lyon, was taken by train to Grandvillars, southeast of Belfort, only on 14 to 18 August, and then joined the Mulhouse offensive.

choices.text: Act on Gauthier’s letter: order Admiral Lapeyrère to hunt down the Goeben without waiting for a declaration of war
choices.why: A preemptive strike is the only way to protect the transports
choices.after: The French fleet raced south from Toulon, but the Goeben was faster. The German government cited the French fleet’s movements as a further ground in its declaration of war, and the non-interventionists in London began asking again who had fired first.

note.text: On 27 July the government telegraphed Lyautey, the resident-general in Morocco, to be ready to give up the interior and hold only the main ports. The telegram opened with the sentence 'The fate of Morocco will be settled in Lorraine.' Lyautey sent the troops requested to France but did not abandon his posts in the interior.

FR-11.place: The Quai d’Orsay in Paris and the concentration areas on the eastern frontier
FR-11.title: Plan XVII

map.caption: Plan XVII aimed its offensive at Lorraine and Alsace, but the German right wing came through Liège and swung wide across Belgium.

telegram.from: Letter from the German ambassador, Schoen
telegram.text: French military aircraft flew over Belgium / bombs dropped on railways near Karlsruhe and Nuremberg / in view of these acts of aggression German Empire considers itself in state of war with France

FR-11.scene: Schoen’s letter gave as its ground for war that French aircraft had bombed the railway near Nuremberg, but no such flight had taken place. That afternoon in London, Grey had explained to the House of Commons why Britain would have to act for Belgium and France. Under Joffre’s Plan XVII, five armies are concentrating on the eastern frontier; the First and Second Armies are to advance into Lorraine, and the VII Corps toward Mulhouse in Alsace. Behind the infantry in red trousers and blue greatcoats, the 75mm field guns stand in line.

voices.text: The French army wins only by attacking. By advancing into Lorraine we can cut the German center. The Germans who pass through Belgium will stay east of the Meuse.
If the German right wing swings wide west of the Meuse, the Fifth Army cannot stop it alone. We must not leave the north bare.

choices.text: Adopt the plan Joffre sought approval for in 1912: enter Belgium ahead of Germany and seize Namur and the Meuse line
choices.why: Holding the key points first lets the neutrality issue wait
choices.after: When French troops crossed the Belgian frontier first, Brussels protested, and the non-interventionists in London cried that it was France that had broken Belgian neutrality. The strongest case for British intervention is gone.

choices.text: Heed Lanrezac’s warning: delay the Lorraine offensive and shift part of the main force north toward the Belgian frontier
choices.why: Stop the enemy’s right wing first, and Paris is saved
choices.after: Joffre reluctantly turned two corps north. The Lorraine offensive was put off, but the French line stood a little thicker in front of the German right wing coming round through Belgium.

choices.text: Launch the offensive into Alsace and Lorraine under Plan XVII, to cut the German center and win back the lost provinces
choices.why: Wars are won by seizing the initiative and attacking
choices.after: On 8 August French troops entered Mulhouse but were driven out two days later, and the Lorraine offensive that began on 14 August was broken at Morhange. Contrary to Joffre’s expectations, the German right wing swung wide through Belgium. On 22 August alone, an estimated 27,000 French soldiers were killed.

note.text: The 1897-model 75mm field gun had a hydropneumatic recoil system that let the barrel slide back and return to its place, so it could fire around 15 rounds a minute without being re-aimed. France had about 4,000 of them but was badly short of heavy artillery compared with Germany.

pressure.title: A Man of Lorraine
pressure.text: Your hometown of Bar-le-Duc was occupied by Prussian troops in 1870, and your family’s house was requisitioned. The statue of Strasbourg on the Place de la Concorde has worn black mourning since 1871. The first offensive of Plan XVII is aimed at the lost provinces of Alsace and Lorraine, and that weighs heavily on the nation and on you. Delay the offensive or change its direction, and the newspapers and parliament will say you are giving up Alsace-Lorraine.

FR-12.title: A Cabinet of Sacred Union
FR-12.event: On 20 August the French offensive in Lorraine was broken at Morhange, and French forces were then driven back in the Ardennes and along the Sambre. The German right wing is coming through Belgium into northern France. Around this time, trains carrying Belgian refugees were arriving in Paris.
FR-12.scene: Yesterday, 25 August, Viviani asked War Minister Messimy to step down, but Messimy refused. An article that Messimy is said to have written and passed on had appeared in Le Matin under a senator’s name, accusing soldiers of the XV Corps, from Provence, of running from the enemy in Lorraine, and the army and opinion in the south were in uproar. In the end the whole cabinet resigned, and Viviani has come to the Élysée with a new list: Briand as deputy prime minister and justice minister, Delcassé at foreign affairs, Millerand at war, Ribot at finance, and the Socialists Jules Guesde and Marcel Sembat brought in as ministers.

voices.who: You (on the small reshuffle of 3 August, in your later memoirs)
voices.text: I would have wished for a broader reshuffle, one that would have allowed the cabinet to represent diverse political opinions and take on the character of national union.
The blame for the defeats lies with incompetent generals. All I did was ask that they be severely punished, and throwing out the war minister in the middle of a war will shake the army.

choices.text: Protect Messimy as he pleads. The generals are to blame for the defeats, and changing war ministers mid-war will shake the army
choices.why: Changing men in a crisis only deepens the upheaval
choices.after: Messimy stayed on, but southern deputies, furious over the XV Corps article, attacked the government fiercely, and Joffre had to issue a separate statement defending the soldiers' honor. The government of national union was formed only weeks later.

choices.text: Approve Viviani’s new list and fight the war with a government of national union that takes in the Socialists Guesde and Sembat
choices.why: A long war can be borne only if all parties share responsibility
choices.after: The second Viviani government took office on 26 August. In this cabinet, which reached from the Socialists to the moderate republicans, Jules Guesde and Marcel Sembat became the first members of the Socialist Party (SFIO) to serve as ministers. Messimy went to the front as a reserve battalion commander, and by the end of the war he was a general commanding a division.

choices.text: Make Clemenceau, who refused to join the cabinet, prime minister himself, with a war cabinet to drive army and parliament
choices.why: A war calls for the strongest hand available
