choices.after: Clemenceau had resented you deeply ever since the presidential election of 1913. As soon as he took office he pushed you back into a ceremonial role and began to drive even general headquarters. In the event, you called him to be prime minister three years later, in November 1917.

note.text: Jules Guesde, the socialist who had led French Marxism since the 1880s, had attended the International Socialist Bureau meeting in Brussels on 29 July alongside Jaurès. His entry into the cabinet as a minister without portfolio a month later became a symbol of the 'sacred union.'

epilogues.A: Until his term ended in 1920, Poincaré heard himself called both 'the president who prevented the war' and 'the man from Lorraine who abandoned Russia.' Alsace-Lorraine was still German, and the statue of Strasbourg on the Place de la Concorde kept its black mourning. The roughly 1.3 million French soldiers who died in the war as it actually happened would have lived on.
epilogues.B: The Austrian army halted at Belgrade and France escaped war, but in St Petersburg resentment grew that France had once again left Russia to stand alone. Poincaré tried to shore up the alliance by enlarging the Russian railway loans and keeping the three-year service law, but at home he was attacked by both the nationalists and the Socialists over 'the price of peace.' The Balkan question was left unresolved and passed on to the next crisis.
epilogues.C: France watched the war in the east from its frontier, weapons in hand. The Franco-Russian alliance that had stood since 1894 collapsed, and whether Germany won or lost in the east, France would have to stand alone in Europe without allies. The charge that a president from Lorraine had not fought for Alsace-Lorraine would likely have followed Poincaré for the rest of his life.
epilogues.D: France and Russia fought Germany without Britain. Without the protection of the British fleet, the northern coast of France and the Channel lay open to the German navy, and German propaganda that France had been first to break Belgian neutrality swayed opinion in neutral countries. Whether Paris could have held at the Battle of the Marne in September 1914 without the British Expeditionary Force beside it, no one can say.
epilogues.E: Your message to parliament on 4 August 1914 declared that France 'will be heroically defended by all her sons; nothing will break their sacred union before the enemy.' In early September the government moved to Bordeaux, and Joffre stopped the German army on the Marne. The war lasted four years and three months and killed about 1.3 million French soldiers, and the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 returned Alsace-Lorraine to France. In November 1917 Poincaré made his old rival Clemenceau prime minister and fought the war to its end; after the war, as prime minister, he occupied the Ruhr (1923), and his opponents called him 'Poincaré-la-Guerre.'
epilogues.F: The crisis of 1914 passed, but France prepared for the next war with the three-year service law and railway loans to Russia, and the German general staff believed it had to fight before Russia’s 'Great Programme' was completed in 1917. When crisis returned a few years later, Europe’s armies were bigger and faster. The time Poincaré had won may have bought not peace but a longer run-up to a larger war.

dossier.t: Born on 20 August 1860 at Bar-le-Duc in the Meuse department of Lorraine, the son of a civil engineer, you are 53 in July 1914. In the war of 1870 Prussian troops requisitioned the family home, and a story goes that the following year the boy named his dog 'Bismarck.' The mathematician Henri Poincaré (died 1912) was your cousin, and the physicist Lucien Poincaré is your brother. True to your training as a lawyer, you read documents meticulously and rarely show emotion, and you were often described as cold and exacting. The diary you kept daily and the multivolume memoirs you published after the war, Au service de la France, are key sources for July 1914.

Your wife Henriette, the daughter of an Italian-born coachman, had been married twice before, which made her a frequent target of newspaper gossip. The two of you married in a civil ceremony in 1904, and only after your election as president, once her first husband’s death had been confirmed, did you quietly marry in church. Prime Minister Viviani was a celebrated orator but highly strung; in your memoirs you wrote that his excessive sensitivity often caused him torment. Paléologue, the ambassador to Russia, was your schoolmate at the Lycée Louis-le-Grand in Paris. Your rival Clemenceau never forgave you for standing in the 1913 presidential election instead of abiding by the result of the republicans' preliminary ballot.

Your greatest fear is that France will have to face Germany alone. With a population more than 20 million smaller than Germany’s, France tried to close the gap through the alliance with Russia and the three-year service law of 1913. When the left, which wanted to revise the three-year law, won heavily in the general election of April and May 1914, the Ribot government you had appointed fell on 12 June, the day it first faced the Chamber, and the next day Viviani, who promised to apply the law as it stood, took over. At home, all summer long, the Senate’s defense budget debate, the income tax bill and the Caillaux affair shook the government. Your hope is that Britain will come down clearly on France’s side, and some read in you, a man of Lorraine, the hope that Alsace-Lorraine would one day return.

movers.intro: How much responsibility Poincaré bore for the war of July 1914 was disputed from the moment the war ended. His opponents called him 'Poincaré-la-Guerre,' and he answered the charge in several volumes of memoirs. The main views are as follows.
views: John Keiger: sees Poincaré’s diplomacy not as a war of revenge to regain Alsace-Lorraine but as a defensive policy of preserving the balance of power with Germany through alliance and armaments. He thinks it goes too far to explain his decisions by his Lorraine origins.

Christopher Clark: argues that from his time as prime minister in 1912 Poincaré tightened the alliance so that even a crisis beginning in the Balkans would be treated as a matter for the Franco-Russian alliance, and that the firm stance he took in St Petersburg in July 1914 strengthened the hand of Russia’s hard-liners.

Gerd Krumeich: analyzing the domestic politics of the three-year service law of 1913, he argues that the law was both a response to German army increases and a political decision meant to show Russia France’s resolve.

Jean-Jacques Becker: showed that in August 1914 most French people answered the mobilization less with enthusiasm than with resignation and a sense of duty. The general strike or refusal to mobilize that the government feared did not happen.
movers.note: Many scholars point out that Poincaré’s memoirs, written at the height of the war-guilt controversy, are strongly self-justifying and should be read against the original diary held at the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
